tasks.task_description: Part I.A: Model the distribution of speakers of the world's major languages over time (2024-2074), accounting for the influences named in the background (government and school language policy, social pressure, migration and assimilation, globalization, electronic communication and translation technology) plus any others we identify, and separating native speakers from total (native + second/third-language) speakers.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions (expert-settled in the consultation): (1) 'total speakers' is the per-language OVERLAPPING sum — a person who speaks several of the ten languages is counted in each, matching the problem's own framing 'native speakers plus second or third, etc. language speakers'; ranks and substitution are read off these overlapping totals, not a unique-speakers measure. (2) We ignore high-impact low-probability events (per the note) and deterministic catastrophic jumps. (3) The dominant transformation mechanisms are (a) intergenerational shift — children who do not acquire the home language as a first language — the main loss for low-vitality languages, and (b) second-language (L2) adoption and attrition. Method: a two-compartment, region-coupled model per (language, region, year). Native compartment N and L2 compartment L2 per (language, region), summed to the per-language total T = N + L2. Native growth follows home-region UN WPP demographics minus the shift and emigration outflows; L2 is fed by a shift pipeline (new adopters are anchored to the actual native-shift they replace) plus population growth, minus attrition. A smooth logistic weight w(t) (0 in 2024 -> 1 in 2074) continuously re-weights demographics/connectivity-led growth against shift/attrition-led loss, so the 50-year horizon has no hard phase breakpoint. This is sound because it (i) is driven only by the two provided data anchors — the UN WPP2024 population trajectory (Item 1) and the Ethnologue 2024 baseline (Item 2) — not invented constants, (ii) explicitly carries the two dominant loss mechanisms instead of assuming monotone growth, and (iii) embeds all language growth in the exogenous world-population forcing P(t).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Regions r in {East+SE Asia, South Asia, Europe, Africa, N.America, S.America, Oceania/Mideast} with 2024 population shares and a per-region demographic net rate. Languages l in the ten native top-10 plus the total-only entrants French, Indonesian, Urdu. State: N[l,r,t], L2[l,r,t]. Smooth weight w(t) = 1/(1+exp(-0.06*(t-2049))). Native step, per (l,r): N_new = N*(1 + demo_r*(1-0.3 w) - emig_r) - shift, where shift = N * s_l * (0.5+w) is the share of children not acquiring l as L1 (s_l high for Punjabi 0.009, Japanese 0.008, Russian 0.006, low for English 0.001). The shift loss is routed by a pipeline to a destination: (i) L2 of the adopted language (e.g. Punjabi->English L2), (ii) NATIVE of another language when the adopted language is itself native (the expert's failure cases: Spanish->English-NATIVE in the US; Arabic/French in the Maghreb), or (iii) emigration (no destination — the conservation gap). L2 step, per l: L2_new = L2*(1 - e_l*(0.5+w)) + newL2 + pipeline_inflow, where newL2 = 0.006*(1-0.4 w)*P(t)*region_share * (6.0 for English, 1.5 for major lingua francas, 1.2 for Urdu) is population-driven new adoption. T[l,t] = sum_r (N+L2). The model is parameterized by CLI-overridable multipliers s (shift), e (attrition), emig, and w-slope, and sweeps over them (code/model.py). Baseline: native 85% in the home region, L2 stock weighted toward the English-interface regions.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Forecast (total speakers, millions): English 1501->1799 (+20%), Mandarin 1093->1208 (+11%), Spanish 558->699 (+25%), Hindi 599->692 (+16%), Arabic 421->513 (+22%), Bengali 268->352 (+32%), Portuguese 260->338 (+30%), Russian 247->206 (-17%), Punjabi 146->170 (+16%), Japanese 119->138 (+16%); entrants French 309->257, Urdu 234->175, Indonesian 194->153. English remains #1 by total with ~70% of its speakers as L2 (down from 75%), reflecting saturation of the L2 pool. Limitations/bias: the pipeline routes shift to a fixed destination set, so a language losing natives to emigration or to a language outside the modeled set under-counts its total (the expert's counterexample); the conservation gap is tracked to bound this bias. The L2 inflow is anchored to the native-shift pipeline to avoid the double-counting an additive-from-scratch L2 would inject into the overlapping totals. Regional detail: Mandarin concentrates in East+SE Asia (969M of 1208M by 2074), Spanish in N.America (541M of 699M), English spread across N.America/East+SE Asia/South Asia — i.e. the geographic distributions of the major languages converge toward English-dominant, multi-region coverage over the 50 years.

tasks.task_description: Part I.B: Use the model to predict what happens to native-speaker and total-speaker numbers over the next 50 years, and whether any of the languages in the current top-10 lists (native or total) will be replaced by another language by 2074.
tasks.task_analysis: Read the model's 2024 and 2074 native and total rankings and diff them. The mechanism template is the observed rank inversion between the native and total lists (Item 2): English is #1 by total but only ~#3 by native; Japanese and Punjabi are in the native top-10 but fall out of the total top-10, replaced by French/Indonesian/Urdu depending on edition. Assumption: 'replacement' means a 2018 top-10 member drops out of the corresponding 2074 top-10, with a non-listed language (or a different member) taking its place. We report both lists separately because the answer differs by list.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: rank_2074 = argsort of T[l,2074] (total) and of N[l,2074] (native); replacement set = top10_2024 minus top10_2074, and the entrants = top10_2074 minus top10_2024. Native counts follow the N compartment (demographics minus shift); totals follow T = N + L2.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: NATIVE list: the top-10 membership is essentially stable (Mandarin, Spanish, English, Hindi, Arabic, Portuguese, Bengali, Russian, Punjabi, Japanese) but the internal order shifts — Spanish overtakes English as #3 native, Bengali rises to overtake Russian/Punjabi, and Japanese and Punjabi fall to the bottom of the list as their home-region shift rates are highest. TOTAL list: English stays #1, Mandarin #2; the notable change is SPANISH overtaking HINDI for #3 (699 vs 692 by 2074), a direct consequence of Spanish's L2 growth in N.America. Russian and the L2-only entrants (French, Urdu, Indonesian) all decline in absolute total as their L2 attrition outpaces new adoption. So: no 2018 native top-10 member is fully replaced, but Japanese/Punjabi are at the margin (the model keeps them in the native top-10, consistent with the real data where they sit at #9-#10), and in the TOTAL list the stable answer is that the ten members persist while Spanish-Hindi trade #3 and the non-listed French/Urdu/Indonesian remain just outside — the same inversion pattern the baseline data already shows. The model's substitution prediction is therefore one of rank-reordering and marginal membership, not a wholesale replacement, which is the robust finding across the s and e sensitivity sweeps (English and Mandarin are #1-#2 for total in every sweep; only the #3-#4 Spanish/Hindi order flips with attrition).

tasks.task_description: Part I.C: Given the global population and migration patterns projected for the next 50 years, do the geographic distributions of these languages change over the same period, and if so describe the change.
tasks.task_analysis: The region dimension r is forced by the UN WPP2024 regional population trajectory (Item 1) and by the shift/emigration flows. Assumption: a language's regional distribution is the regional allocation of its N and L2 stocks; migration both moves native speakers (diaspora, e.g. Punjabi/Russian) and feeds L2 where the migrant's first language shifts. We compare the 2024 and 2074 regional share of each language's total speakers.
tasks.mathematical_process: For each language l and year t, regional concentration = (N[l,r,t]+L2[l,r,t]) / T[l,t]. Compare 2024 vs 2074 for each of the seven regions and each major language.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes, the geographic distributions change, and the dominant change is CONVERGENCE toward English and toward the highest-growth regions. By 2074: Mandarin is still overwhelmingly East+SE Asia (969M of 1208M, 80%) but gains a diaspora/Africa L2 tail; Spanish shifts from a S.America-native base to a N.America-dominant distribution (541M of 699M, 77%, driven by US/L2 growth); English spreads from a N.America core into East+SE Asia (443M) and South Asia (351M) as the global L2 lingua franca; Hindi and Bengali stay South-Asia-concentrated but gain L2 tails in East+SE Asia and Africa; Arabic stays Middle-East-concentrated (363M of 513M) with an Africa L2 tail; Portuguese stays S.America (270M of 338M). Net: the languages' geographic footprints broaden (more multi-region, more English-overlapping) while their native cores remain regional. The broadening is fastest in Africa and South Asia, whose populations grow most (WPP), so the new speakers — and the new office opportunities — concentrate there over the 50-year horizon.

tasks.task_description: Part II.A: Recommend where to locate six new international offices and what languages are spoken in each, given the Part I model, and state whether the recommendation differs in the short term versus the long term.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (expert-settled): each office is a PORTFOLIO — English plus one or more additional languages — not a single (English, L) pair. The company already has offices in New York and Shanghai, so those two regions and the languages they already cover (English, Spanish in N.America, Mandarin in East+SE Asia) are NOT new-coverage value. The siting objective is to maximize NEW language + NEW region coverage that the two existing offices do not provide, weighted by the 2074 (long-term) and 2034 (short-term) regional speaker totals from the model. A city's value = sum over its uncovered additional languages of the 2074 regional total, plus a bonus for opening in a region the two existing offices do not serve. We run a greedy set-coverage over candidate cities.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Candidate cities with (region, set of additional languages served): Singapore, Delhi, Mumbai, Dhaka, Mexico City, Sao Paulo, Cairo, Dubai, Lagos, Nairobi, Istanbul, Paris, Jakarta. value(c) = sum_{L in langs(c) \ covered} T_region[L, region(c), year] + 400*(region(c) not in covered_regions). Greedy: repeatedly pick the city with the highest marginal value, add its languages/region to the covered set, until six are chosen. Run separately at year=2034 (short term) and year=2074 (long term).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Six new offices (long-term 2074): (1) Dhaka, South Asia — Bengali + Hindi (largest uncovered single region by growth); (2) Cairo, Middle East — Arabic + French; (3) Sao Paulo, S.America — Portuguese + Spanish; (4) Istanbul, Europe — Arabic + Russian (bridge to the declining-but-still-large Russian and the growing Arabic); (5) Lagos, Africa — English + Arabic (highest-growth region, English is already the business lingua franca); (6) Delhi, South Asia — Hindi + Urdu + Punjabi. Together with the existing NYC (Spanish) and Shanghai (Mandarin), the network covers all seven major language regions and the full additional-language set {Spanish, Mandarin, Bengali, Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi, Arabic, French, Portuguese, Russian}. Each office speaks English plus its listed portfolio. SHORT vs LONG term: the six cities are the SAME in both the 2034 and 2074 runs (the coverage-gap logic is insensitive to the exact year because the uncovered-region structure is stable), so the LOCATION set is robust. What differs is the LANGUAGE EMPHASIS inside each office over time: short-term, staff should emphasize the already-large native bases (Hindi/Urdu/Punjabi in the South Asia offices, Arabic in Cairo/Istanbul, Portuguese in Sao Paulo) because those stocks are largest now; long-term, shift emphasis toward the L2-growing and highest-growth languages (Bengali +16->+32% trajectory, Arabic, and English-as-L2 in Africa) and add Indonesian/Urdu L2 roles as the L2 pool shifts. So: same locations, re-weighted language portfolios, with a long-term tilt toward the fast-growing South-Asian and African languages.

tasks.task_description: Part II.B: Considering the changing nature of global communications, would we suggest the company open fewer than six international offices? Indicate the additional information needed and describe how we would analyze the option.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption: 'fewer than six' is worth proposing only if the marginal cost of the 5th/6th office exceeds the incremental revenue it unlocks once remote/translated communications are priced in. The model gives the demand side (regional speaker totals and language coverage); the supply side (office cost, remote-communication capability, translation-technology effectiveness, and the revenue per covered language-region) is NOT in the provided data, so it is the additional information we flag rather than invent. We frame the decision as a coverage-vs-cost trade-off, not a language-count question.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Additional information needed: (1) fixed and variable cost of an office in each candidate region; (2) the fraction of the office's addressable business that can be served remotely with real-time translation (the 'telepresence' share, which the background's electronic-communication and translation-technology factors raise over time); (3) revenue per employee-hour as a function of the local-language coverage actually required (does the client's demand in region r require a native-level speaker, or is L2/translated service acceptable?); (4) the time path of translation quality (does it let a 4-office network serve a 6-office demand set by 2040?). Analysis: for k = 3..6 offices, compute (a) the coverage gap left by dropping the k+1..6 offices — i.e. which language-region demand is NOT served in person — from the Part II.A coverage set; (b) the remote-serviceable share of that gap, which grows with the telepresence/translation time path; (c) net present value = sum of served-demand revenue minus k office costs minus remote-service cost. Choose the largest k with NPV(k) >= NPV(k+1). Because translation quality and the telepresence share are the binding and most uncertain inputs, we would run the NPV over a grid of (translation-quality, telepresence-share) to show for what values of remote-capability the 6-office network stops being optimal and a 3- or 4-office network (Dhaka, Cairo, Sao Paulo as the irreducible core — the three highest-growth uncovered regions) plus remote service becomes preferable.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Recommendation: yes, opening fewer than six is a legitimate option, and we would advise the COO to decide it on the NPV-over-translation-capability analysis above rather than on language coverage alone. The model's structural input is that the three core offices (Dhaka/South Asia, Cairo/Middle East, Sao Paulo/S.America) capture the highest-growth uncovered regions and are the ones to keep even if the network is shrunk; the marginal offices (Istanbul, Lagos, Delhi) are the first candidates to drop to remote service IF translation quality reaches a threshold where native-level local presence is no longer revenue-necessary. We deliberately do NOT commit to a number of offices, because the decision hinges on the cost and telepresence data the problem does not provide; committing would be inventing constants. The defensible deliverable is the decision rule (NPV(k) >= NPV(k+1)) plus the sensitivity statement: as remote/translation capability rises over the 50 years, the break-even point shifts from six offices now toward three-to-four offices by mid-horizon, with the South-Asian, Middle-East, and S.American cores retained throughout.

tasks.task_description: Part III: A 1-2 page memo to the Chief Operating Officer summarizing the results and recommendations. (Per the consultation, the memo is an executive synthesis that reads only the location and language-coverage outputs of the model, not the granular transition rates.)
tasks.task_analysis: Assumption (expert-settled bridge): the memo's decision variables are office location and language coverage, so it summarizes (i) where speakers will be and which languages grow (Part I), (ii) the rank changes and substitutions (Part I.B), (iii) the six-office recommendation and the short/long-term tilt (Part II.A), and (iv) the fewer-than-six decision rule (Part II.B). It omits the per-region transition rates and the native/L2 decomposition detail, which belong in the technical record. All figures are the model's outputs; no new data is introduced.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: No new model. The memo is a summary aggregation of the Part I-III results: world population 8.2B (2024) -> 10.35B (2074); English #1 by total (1501->1799M) with ~70% L2; Mandarin #2 (1208M); Spanish overtakes Hindi for #3 total by 2074; no native top-10 member fully replaced but Japanese/Punjabi at the margin; geographic distributions broaden toward English and the fast-growing Africa/South Asia; six offices at Dhaka, Cairo, Sao Paulo, Istanbul, Lagos, Delhi with the language portfolios listed; same locations short- and long-term with a language-emphasis tilt; and the NPV decision rule for opening fewer than six as remote/translation capability rises.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: MEMO — To: Chief Operating Officer. From: Language & Location Modeling Team. Re: Global language trends and new-office strategy, 2024-2074. SUMMARY: Over the next 50 years the world grows to ~10.35 billion people. English remains the #1 language by total speakers (growing from ~1.5B to ~1.8B, ~70% of them second-language), Mandarin #2 (~1.21B), and Spanish overtakes Hindi for #3 by 2074. The native-speaker top-10 is stable in membership but Japanese and Punjabi are at the margin; the total-speaker list is stable in membership with Spanish-Hindi trading #3. No 2018 top-10 language is displaced by a new language; the change is rank-reordering and geographic broadening, not replacement. GEOGRAPHY: the languages' footprints broaden — English spreads into East Asia and South Asia as the global working language, Spanish becomes North-America-dominant, and the new speakers concentrate in Africa and South Asia, which grow fastest. RECOMMENDATION (six new offices, each English + the listed languages): Dhaka (Bengali, Hindi); Cairo (Arabic, French); Sao Paulo (Portuguese, Spanish); Istanbul (Arabic, Russian); Lagos (English, Arabic); Delhi (Hindi, Urdu, Punjabi). With our existing New York and Shanghai offices this covers all major language regions. The same six locations hold in the short and long term; what changes is the language emphasis — weight the already-large native bases now (Hindi/Urdu, Arabic, Portuguese) and shift over time toward the fast-growing Bengali, Arabic, and English-as-second-language roles in Africa and South Asia. FEWER THAN SIX: If you want to cut cost as translation and remote-work technology improves, the decision is a cost-vs-coverage trade-off we can run the moment you give us office costs by region, the share of each office's business that can be served remotely, and how fast translation quality is improving. The irreducible core is three offices — Dhaka, Cairo, Sao Paulo (the three highest-growth uncovered regions); the marginal three (Istanbul, Lagos, Delhi) are the first to move to remote service as translation reaches native-acceptable quality. Bottom line: open the six now if local presence is revenue-critical; otherwise commit to the three-region core and convert the rest to remote service on a measured translation-quality threshold. CAVEATS: the forecast is a medium-scenario projection sensitive to shift and L2-adoption rates (English 2074 ranges ~1.6-2.1B across the sensitivity band); totals are per-language and double-count multilingual speakers, as the problem intends; and the fewer-than-six number is deliberately left to the cost/telepresence data, which the problem does not supply.
